classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish supplied inputs from outputs, substitute numerical or algebraic arguments, and solve a directly specified linear equation for each preimage.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d evaluate inputs; parts e–f solve for preimages using the demonstrated input/output distinction.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 substitutes the input into a linear rule or sets the rule equal to the supplied output. Example 2 substitutes an algebraic argument and expands.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution, expansion of linear expressions and two-step linear preimage equations.

classification.difficultyReason: Quadratic substitution with a reciprocal argument and factorised quadratic preimage equations.

questions.mappingNote: Parts c and d extend the algebraic-input example; parts e and f use the same quadratic preimage method.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the complete input into each occurrence of x, simplify, and solve preimage equations by rearranging and factorising as in Example 2.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Quadratic substitution with a reciprocal argument and factorised quadratic preimage equations.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate reciprocals and reverse the reciprocal rule for specified outputs; all inputs and outputs are explicit and nonzero.

questions.mappingNote: The same function-notation operations are applied to a reciprocal rule; reciprocal arithmetic is prerequisite knowledge.
questions.methodNote: Use the substitution and preimage distinction from Example 1; retain the explicit input restriction, consistent with Example 5.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate reciprocals and solve simple reciprocal equations with nonzero inputs.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate positive square roots or square a supplied positive output to recover its input, using the stated domain.

questions.mappingNote: The operations extend the input/output method to the positive square-root rule using the inverse relationship between squaring and square roots.
questions.methodNote: Substitute known inputs and set the function rule equal to known outputs, as in Example 1. Respect the stated domain restriction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate square roots of perfect squares and invert a square-root rule.

classification.difficultyReason: Read images, preimages and range from a supplied graph, and use one output as the next input.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly apply Example 4's graphical methods; the graph's codomain must not be substituted for its actual range.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 reads an image at a fixed x, finds preimages at a fixed y, evaluates a nested function in two successive readings and reads the attained y-values for the range.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read images, preimages and range from a supplied graph, and use one output as the next input.

classification.difficultyReason: Read inputs and outputs from a piecewise-linear graph, recognise an interval of inputs with the same output, and evaluate a nested function.

questions.mappingNote: Page 3 Example 4 directly demonstrates these four graphical tasks. Pages 1 and 2 establish input, output, image and range terminology.
questions.methodNote: Use the graph to read the output at a given input, find inputs at a specified height, evaluate nested function notation by successive readings, and identify the complete set of output values.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read inputs and outputs from a piecewise-linear graph, recognise an interval of inputs with the same output, and evaluate a nested function.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate an area function, solve for a radius and rearrange the rule to express radius as a function of area.

questions.mappingNote: Page 1 introduces radius-to-area functions and demonstrates input substitution and solving for an input. Page 2 reinforces function notation and distinguishes inputs from outputs. Part (c) directly assesses changing the subject of the area formula.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the input into the function rule; for a specified output, set the function rule equal to that output and solve. Rearrange the circle-area rule and take the non-negative square root to obtain the radius.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate an area function, solve for a radius and rearrange the rule to express radius as a function of area.

classification.difficultyReason: To minimise the input for digit sum 100, infer the minimum number of digits from the bound of 9 per digit, then minimise the leading digit while keeping the remaining sum achievable. Part (b) provides a smaller precursor.

questions.mappingNote: Function notation is directly assessed in all three parts. The smallest-input reasoning uses decimal place value and the maximum digit value of 9; it does not require an inverse-function rule.
questions.methodNote: Treat a function as an input-output rule and evaluate it by applying its definition. This question supplies its own digit-sum definition and numerical demonstration.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate a defined function and reason about the smallest input with a specified digit sum.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine an output interval and solve a compound inequality for the corresponding input interval.

questions.mappingNote: Question 10(a) applies the range interpretation and restricted linear-function endpoints illustrated in Example 3; question 10(b) extends the input-solving method of Example 1 to a compound inequality.
questions.methodNote: Use substitution to evaluate endpoint images, distinguish inputs from outputs, and express the resulting sets in interval notation. Solve the input restriction by substituting the function rule and applying inverse operations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine an output interval and solve a compound inequality for the corresponding input interval.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish output sets from input sets, locate the quadratic minimum on a restricted interval, and intersect the input regions satisfying two output bounds.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) asks for the outputs on a restricted input interval; part (b) asks for inputs whose quadratic outputs satisfy a double inequality. Quadratic inequalities are the most advanced directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Use substitution and factorisation as in Examples 1–2, and interpret restricted outputs and input sets using the graph and range methods in Examples 3–4.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Finds a restricted quadratic range and the input intervals satisfying two output bounds.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch restricted linear, quadratic and cubic functions, distinguishing included endpoints, excluded endpoints and discrete domains.

questions.mappingNote: Each part applies Example 3's restricted-graph method: (a–e) straight lines, (f–h,k) parabolas, (i–j) cubics, and (l–m) isolated points for finite domains. Domain and range in interval or set notation are the most advanced shared assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 3 sketches the familiar function graph restricted to its stated input domain, marks included and excluded endpoints, and reads the range as the actual outputs. Page 2 distinguishes domain, codomain and range.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch restricted linear, quadratic and cubic functions, distinguishing included endpoints, excluded endpoints and discrete domains.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the supplied floor definition, recognising that a negative noninteger rounds to the lower integer, then subtract a previously evaluated floor value.

questions.mappingNote: Function notation is the closest catalogue match because every part evaluates the explicitly defined floor function; part f also subtracts its output.
questions.methodNote: Use the embedded floor-function definition: identify the integer n satisfying n ≤ x < n + 1, then substitute the resulting output in part f. Pages 1 and 2 establish function inputs and outputs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate a supplied function definition at positive, integer and negative inputs.

classification.difficultyReason: Restrict a straight-line graph to a half-open interval and explain why its excluded upper endpoint prevents a maximum.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses domain and range in interval notation, including the effect of an excluded endpoint on attainment of a maximum.
questions.methodNote: Use the specified input set as the domain, restrict the graph to that set, mark included and excluded endpoints, and read the range as the actual outputs. Example 3 models this method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Restrict a straight-line graph to a half-open interval and explain why its excluded upper endpoint prevents a maximum.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert domain and range endpoints into two points and determine a linear rule; the supplied gradient hint directs reversing the endpoint pairing for the second rule.

questions.mappingNote: The task reverses the restricted-linear-function example by requiring a rule from domain and range endpoints. Matching the endpoints in increasing and decreasing order gives the two gradient signs.
questions.methodNote: Function notation associates each input with an output; domain restrictions select the permitted inputs, and the range comprises their actual outputs. Example 3 demonstrates endpoint-based domain and range interpretation for a restricted linear function.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct two linear rules from specified domain and range endpoints, considering both gradient signs.

classification.difficultyReason: Recover the function rule by substituting a new variable for its shifted argument.

questions.mappingNote: Evaluating at an algebraic argument is the closest catalogue skill: the task reverses the given shifted-argument representation to recover the rule.
questions.methodNote: Use function notation and substitute an algebraic argument, expanding and simplifying as demonstrated in Example 2(b). Follow the question's explicit change-of-variable hint.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recover the function rule by substituting a new variable for its shifted argument.

classification.difficultyReason: Recover the function rule by reversing a linear algebraic argument.

questions.mappingNote: Pages 1–2 establish function notation and substitution, including Example 2(b). The matching teacher solution explicitly uses a=2x+3. Page 3 supplies graphical context but no additional method needed here.
questions.methodNote: Use the input–output interpretation and substitution of an algebraic argument. Introduce a new input variable, rearrange the argument, and substitute into the supplied output expression.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recover the function rule by reversing a linear algebraic argument.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the applicable linear rule, sketch restricted branches with correct endpoints, and combine their ranges.

questions.mappingNote: Question 1 uses the same interval-based substitution and restricted-branch sketching method with two linear rules; the requested range follows from the outputs on those branches.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 selects a defining rule from the input interval and sketches each defining graph only on its assigned interval.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select the applicable linear rule, sketch restricted branches with correct endpoints, and combine their ranges.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the appropriate rule, join a constant branch to a restricted parabola, and determine the range.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 directly applies this method to a constant branch and a translated quadratic branch; the graph then establishes the range.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 selects a rule by checking the input against its interval and sketches each defining expression only on the stated domain interval.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select the appropriate rule, join a constant branch to a restricted parabola, and determine the range.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine three domain-restricted rules, solve for inputs and identify the range.

questions.mappingNote: Question 3 directly assesses graphing three restricted pieces, including endpoints, and using the resulting function to find inputs and range.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 selects the applicable rule from the input interval and sketches only the corresponding portion of each defining graph. Example 2 illustrates joined linear pieces and a vertex.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine three domain-restricted rules, solve for inputs and identify the range.

classification.difficultyReason: Draw each constant branch on its specified half-line, distinguish open and closed endpoints, and identify the two actual output values.

questions.mappingNote: Question 4 applies the same interval-by-interval graphing method to constant branches. Graph-piecewise is the closest catalogue skill and directly covers endpoint inclusion and range.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 selects the defining rule from the input interval and sketches only the corresponding portion of each defining graph. Example 2 reinforces the treatment of the x<0 and x>=0 branches.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch two constant branches, distinguish the open and closed endpoints, and identify the two output values.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch three constant pieces with correctly included and excluded endpoints, then identify the range.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 applies the same interval-selection method to constant expressions, with endpoint inclusion determined by a≤x≤b.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 selects the defining expression for each domain interval and sketches only the corresponding portion of its graph.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch three constant pieces with correctly included and excluded endpoints, then identify the range.

classification.difficultyReason: For f(-a)=f(a), recognise that nonzero opposite inputs use opposite branches, solve under sign conditions, and check zero separately because its branch assignment differs.

questions.mappingNote: Question 6 uses the same branch-selection and restricted-graph method. Parts (b) and (c) apply it to equations, checking each solution against its branch condition.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 selects the defining expression from the input interval, substitutes into that expression, and sketches only the permitted portion of each component graph.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires a discontinuous piecewise graph, branch-valid equation solutions and separate sign cases for opposite inputs.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the scaffolded identities and squared-expression hint to justify the triangle inequality, then reframe x as (x-y)+y to obtain a reverse inequality and use symmetry for the other.

questions.mappingNote: The most advanced directly assessed task is proving the triangle inequality and its reverse forms; the earlier parts establish the absolute-value identities needed for those proofs.
questions.methodNote: Example 2 defines absolute value by the cases x<0 and x≥0 and evaluates each using its applicable rule. Question 7 supplies the subsequent proof sequence: compare squares using (a), use the product result in (d), then derive reverse inequalities from (e).

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Seven linked proofs use the piecewise definition, squares and previously established absolute-value results.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch horizontal and vertical translations of a supplied graph, including two combined translations.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d directly assess the taught horizontal and vertical translations; parts e–f combine one of each. graph-function-transformations is the closest catalogue skill. Page 8 was inspected as adjacent transformation context; reflections are not required here.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 teaches vertical translations by adding to the output and horizontal translations through f(x-h), demonstrated by moving a supplied piecewise-linear graph on a unit grid. Apply those point movements directly and join corresponding vertices.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch horizontal and vertical translations of a supplied graph, including two combined translations.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch horizontal and vertical translations, including two combined translations, of a supplied segmented graph.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d directly assess single translations; e–f combine horizontal and vertical translations. The closest primary catalogue skill is graph-function-transformations.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 teaches translating every point horizontally for f(x-h) and vertically for f(x)+k. Page 11 demonstrates applying successive transformations to the complete graph.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch horizontal and vertical translations, including two combined translations, of a supplied segmented graph.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare the original graph and three reflected graphs on one set of axes.

questions.mappingNote: Each requested graph directly uses the coordinate reflection rules and graphical method demonstrated on teaching page 8.
questions.methodNote: Reflect in the y-axis for f(-x), in the x-axis for -f(x), and in both axes for -f(-x).

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare the original graph and three reflected graphs on one set of axes.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch and distinguish an original piecewise-linear graph and three axis reflections on shared axes.

questions.mappingNote: Question 4 directly applies these three reflection rules to the supplied graph; part (a) retains the original.
questions.methodNote: Page 108 explains reflections in the x-axis and y-axis through point images, and reflection in both axes as a 180-degree rotation. Example 1 sketches the transformed piecewise-linear graphs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch and distinguish an original piecewise-linear graph and three axis reflections on shared axes.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply vertical and horizontal dilation factors to a supplied graph, including reciprocal horizontal factors.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 directly assesses the vertical and horizontal dilation methods of Example 3 using a V-shaped unit-grid graph with vertex at the origin. The supplied graph was independently read as (-2,2), (0,0), (2,2), and each transformed endpoint was derived before comparison with the teacher diagrams.
questions.methodNote: Page 110 defines vertical dilation as (a,f(a)) to (a,cf(a)) and horizontal dilation for f(cx) as (a,f(a)) to (a/c,f(a)). Example 3 sketches the same four dilation forms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply vertical and horizontal dilation factors to a supplied graph, including reciprocal horizontal factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply vertical and horizontal dilation factors to a supplied graph, including reciprocal horizontal factors.

questions.mappingNote: Question 6 applies the Example 3 graphical coordinate method to a rising segment followed by a horizontal segment; dilate-function-graphs directly matches all four parts.
questions.methodNote: Page 10 teaches vertical dilation by multiplying ordinates by c and horizontal dilation by multiplying abscissae by 1/c for y=f(cx). Example 3 demonstrates precisely the four requested transformations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply vertical and horizontal dilation factors to a supplied graph, including reciprocal horizontal factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch individual transformations and two combinations from a supplied piecewise-linear graph.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d use the translations illustrated on page 9; e–f use the dilation rules and Example 3 on page 10; g–h use the axis reflections on page 8; i–j use the combinations and ordering guidance on page 11. The closest primary skill assesses the combined transformations in i and j.
questions.methodNote: Transform the supplied graph directly: change y-coordinates for vertical transformations and x-coordinates for horizontal transformations. Apply the dilation before the vertical translation in combined parts.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch individual transformations and two combinations from a supplied piecewise-linear graph.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketches include individual transformations and combinations of reflection, dilation and translation.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 continues Section C before the 21D band. Its answer set is Section C, question 8, spanning teacher pages 33–34. The required envelope topicId is retained, while the source identity records 21C. Parts a–d assess translations, e–f dilations, g reflection, and h–j combined transformations.
questions.methodNote: Transform the supplied graph pointwise using the taught translations, axis reflections and vertical or horizontal dilations; combine transformations in the stated order and join corresponding vertices with straight segments.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketches include individual transformations and combinations of reflection, dilation and translation.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch five horizontal translations of the square root function on one coordinate system.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task is translating the square root function, so graph-square-root-function is the closest specific catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the square root curve and horizontal translations, retaining its endpoint and increasing half-parabola shape. Pages 13–14 establish the square root graph and domain; pages 16–17 illustrate graph transformations on shared axes.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch five horizontal translations of the square root function on one coordinate system.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare five horizontal translations of an absolute value graph on one coordinate system.

questions.mappingNote: This question varies only the horizontal shift of y=|x|; absolute value graphing is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 5 compares translated absolute value graphs on shared axes and identifies their translated vertices.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare five horizontal translations of an absolute value graph on one coordinate system.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the specified vertical shifts to the familiar square-root curve, retaining its shape and moving its endpoint to (0,k).

questions.mappingNote: The task assesses graphing translated square root functions, rather than the algebra of functions beginning later on page 19.
questions.methodNote: Use the increasing square root curve introduced on page 13 and vertical translations of its outputs. Page 14 shows domain restrictions and square root endpoints; page 16 confirms the square root curve family.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch five vertical translations of the familiar square root graph on shared axes.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare five vertical translations of an absolute-value graph on shared axes.

questions.mappingNote: Question 4 applies vertical translations to y=|x| while retaining the same branch gradients; graph-absolute-value is the closest directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 3 establishes the V-shaped absolute-value graph. Example 5 and its continuation compare translated absolute-value graphs by locating their vertices on shared axes.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare five vertical translations of an absolute-value graph on shared axes.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare five vertical scalings of the square root graph, including negative and zero factors.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed operation is vertical dilation, with reflection for negative factors, applied to the source square root function.
questions.methodNote: The square root definition uses plotted points joined by a smooth curve, including (0,0), (1,1) and (4,2). Multiply ordinates by c to obtain the five requested graphs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare five vertical scalings of the square root graph, including negative and zero factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare five absolute-value graphs, including vertical dilations, reflections and the zero function.

questions.mappingNote: The assigned task directly assesses graphing absolute-value functions, with dilation and reflection as supporting transformations.
questions.methodNote: Page 15 identifies the absolute-value graph and its origin vertex. Page 16, Example 3, constructs y=c|x| by vertically stretching y=|x|; negative factors additionally reflect across the x-axis.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare five absolute-value graphs, including vertical dilations, reflections and the zero function.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine reciprocal-curve transformations with asymptote placement and intercept calculations, recognising when a domain exclusion or nonzero numerator prevents an intercept.

questions.mappingNote: Each assigned rule is a transformed reciprocal function, so hyperbola-transformations directly assesses the entire shared task. The page's later 21E band does not own this question.
questions.methodNote: Use the reciprocal graph, apply reflection, dilation and translation, identify asymptotes, substitute x=0 for a y-intercept and solve y=0 for an x-intercept. Page 18 Example 7(b) supplies this sequence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch translated, reflected and dilated reciprocal graphs and determine their intercepts and asymptotes.

classification.difficultyReason: Coordinate reflections, scaling and translations for square-root curves, determine endpoints and direction from the radicand, and calculate intercepts while rejecting those outside the domain or output range.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 is a continuation of exercise 21D above the new 21E band. Its combined square-root transformations directly assess apply-combined-transformations, with square-root graphing and natural-domain conditions as secondary skills. Preserve exact surd intercepts. The source uses 'vertices'; solutions identify these as endpoints.
questions.methodNote: Use the square-root parent curve, apply reflections, dilations and translations, identify its included endpoint, require a non-negative radicand, and calculate axial intercepts by setting x=0 or y=0. Pages 13–14 establish the curve and implied domain; page 16 shows reflections; pages 17–18 supply the combined-transformation and intercept method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch sixteen square-root transformations, including combined reflections, dilations and translations, and determine endpoints and intercepts.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret combined transformations of absolute-value graphs, extract scale and translation from linear arguments, and solve both sign branches for intercepts when they exist.

questions.mappingNote: Every part assesses an absolute-value graph. Parts a–d, i and j use translations; e, f, k and l add reflection; g, h, o and p add dilation; m and n use the invariance of absolute value under negation. graph-absolute-value is the closest directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 16 Example 3 teaches vertical stretching of y=|x|. Example 5 on pages 16–17 teaches horizontal and vertical translations of the V-shaped graph. Locate the vertex, apply reflection or dilation where needed, then determine axial intercepts by substitution and setting y=0.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch translated, reflected and dilated absolute-value graphs and calculate their vertices and axial intercepts.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate square-root and denominator requirements into inequalities; the nested radical requires simultaneous inner and outer restrictions, valid squaring, and intersection of the resulting bounds.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and h follow page 14 Example 1(b); b and g use the positivity argument in Example 1(a); c uses the reciprocal restriction on page 13; d applies the square-root domain definition. Parts e and i combine square-root restrictions, while f combines that restriction with a nonzero denominator.
questions.methodNote: Use non-negative radicands and nonzero denominators. Complete the square to show a quadratic is positive everywhere; use the zeros and upward-opening graph to solve quadratic radicand restrictions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines denominator restrictions, quadratic radicands and a nested square root.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine polynomial function rules using addition, subtraction, multiplication and division.

questions.mappingNote: Function notation is the closest supplied catalogue skill for algebraic combinations of functions; the quotient additionally assesses a denominator restriction.
questions.methodNote: Use the pointwise sum, difference and product definitions on page 19 and the quotient definition and nonzero-denominator restriction on page 20. Substitute both rules and simplify, following Example 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine polynomial function rules using addition, subtraction, multiplication and division.

classification.difficultyReason: Forms two-function and nested three-function compositions by substitution and simplification.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess equations of composite functions; parts e and f apply the same taught substitution method twice.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition (f∘g)(x)=f(g(x)); substitute the inner function into the outer rule and simplify, following Example 2 on pages 20–21.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Forms two-function and nested three-function compositions by substitution and simplification.

classification.difficultyReason: Form and simplify two-function and three-function compositions involving a quadratic rule.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts assess equations of composite functions. Parts e and f extend the same taught substitution method to three successive applications.
questions.methodNote: Composition substitutes the inner function's output into the outer rule. Example 2 on pages 20–21 retains the substitution before expanding and simplifying.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form and simplify two-function and three-function compositions involving a quadratic rule.

classification.difficultyReason: Form each composite and solve successive squared equations, retaining both signs where possible and rejecting the negative intermediate value when x squared plus 2 must be positive.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts require forming a composite quadratic rule before solving for its real inputs; composite-function-equations is the closest directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Composition applies the inner function first, then substitutes its output into the outer rule. Example 2 demonstrates substitution and simplification in both orders.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute quadratic rules into one another and solve the resulting equations, rejecting impossible real squares.

classification.difficultyReason: Compose a quadratic with itself and solve the resulting quartic equation by factorisation.

questions.mappingNote: This question applies the same substitution method to self-composition, then solves the resulting equation; composite-functions is the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: The composition definition and Example 2 substitute the inner function into the outer function and simplify.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compose a quadratic with itself and solve the resulting quartic equation by factorisation.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise the inner function output as a useful intermediate unknown, factor the outer quadratic, then solve each resulting quadratic and use discriminants to eliminate branches without real inputs.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts assess composite-function evaluation inside an equation; solving the resulting quadratic branches is secondary.
questions.methodNote: Composition applies the inner function first and substitutes its output into the outer function, as defined on page 20 and demonstrated in Example 2 on pages 20–21. Solve the outer quadratic for the inner output, then solve each resulting equation over the stated real domain.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Solve a quadratic equation in the inner function, then solve the resulting quadratic equations and reject branches with no real inputs.

classification.difficultyReason: Track nested evaluation from the inside out, transferring graph outputs into subsequent inputs and placing the addition at the correct stage.

questions.mappingNote: Page 20 defines composition; page 21 demonstrates successive substitution and reading a composite function through supplied graphs. Question 7 assesses these methods with nested numerical arguments.
questions.methodNote: Composition applies the inner function first. Read each required output from its supplied graph and substitute it as the next function's input.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read values from two piecewise-linear graphs and evaluate nested compositions in the correct order.

classification.difficultyReason: Read two successive function inputs from graphs and retain multiple possible inputs.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 uses the graphical composition introduced on pages 20–21; solving the composite equation requires reversing these successive graphical readings.
questions.methodNote: Composition applies the inner function first. Read the required outer-function inputs from its graph, then read the corresponding original inputs from the inner graph.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read two successive function inputs from graphs and retain multiple possible inputs.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the inner graph's range as the outer graph's input interval, checking internal turning points rather than only endpoint outputs.

questions.mappingNote: Question 9 directly assesses graphical ranges of composite functions; no algebraic piecewise shortcut is needed.
questions.methodNote: Use the inner function's range as the input interval for the outer graph, then read the resulting output interval, as demonstrated in Example 3 on page 21.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read the inner function's range and restrict the outer graph to that interval for four compositions.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires a general proof using the definition of composition rather than evaluating particular functions.

questions.mappingNote: Page 20 defines composition between compatible sets; page 21 demonstrates substitution into the outer function. Question 10 extends this definition to three functions.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition (f∘g)(x)=f(g(x)), applying the inner function first. Establish equality by comparing outputs on the same domain.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires a general proof using the definition of composition rather than evaluating particular functions.

classification.difficultyReason: Exploit the quantifier over every function by choosing a strategically simple function that forces each value of f to equal its input.

questions.mappingNote: The task assesses equality of composite functions for every choice of g; composite-functions is the closest supplied taxonomy skill.
questions.methodNote: Use composition as successive application of functions and prove by contradiction, following the matched teacher proof.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires a proof using the hypothesis for every real-valued function.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise independent repeated-squaring chains, identify their nonsquare starting points, and prove that arbitrary starting values classify all solutions uniquely.

questions.mappingNote: This enrichment question extends the taught composition method to a classification proof. The supplied answer uses arbitrary values at nonsquares and determines values at squares recursively.
questions.methodNote: Use composition as successive application of functions, substituting the inner output into the outer rule. Equating the two compositions gives f(x²)=f(x)².

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Classifies all functions commuting with squaring by identifying arbitrary initial values and proving the resulting construction.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine three coefficients from successive function values and verify the rule for every term.

questions.mappingNote: The principal assessed skill is substitution of an algebraic argument into a function; coefficient determination supports the sequence rule. Pages 19–21 establish algebra of functions and substitution.
questions.methodNote: Use function notation and substitution, retaining exact fractions. Determine coefficients from the supplied input-output pairs and verify the general transition.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine three coefficients from successive function values and verify the rule for every term.
